newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Battling allies hamper Brazil re-election drive.
newsitem.headline: Battling allies hamper Brazil re-election drive.

text.p: The chaos disrupting Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's re-election plan will persist as long as powerful allies remain locked in a power struggle in Congress, political analysts said.

Cardoso's hopes of getting re-election through the Chamber of Deputies in January have been dashed by an unusually fierce battle between Congress' two biggest parties for the presidencies of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

Although government whips say they will put a constitutional amendment allowing re-election to first of two votes on the floor of the lower house on Wednesday, most observers say that looks like a bluff in the current political climate.

"Despite positive talk aimed at keeping the motor running, there's no real chance of re-election being voted (on) tomorrow," political columnist Tereza Cruvinel wrote in Tuesday's edition of newspaper O Globo.
Normally, the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) and the Liberal Front Party (PFL) agree to run one house of Congress each, making elections for the two-year presidencies a formality.

But the PMDB has upset the government's hopes of a trouble-free January by insisting it will put up candidates in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. The elections are due to take place in the first week of February.

The PMDB also told its members not to vote on re-election until Feb. 15, a move seen as countering any behind-the-scenes support from the government for the PFL's candidate in the Senate, powerful political boss Sen. Antonio Carlos Magalhaes.

"Most of the PMDB backs re-election but the president cannot interfere in the (congressional elections) without creating a split," the PMDB's candidate for Senate president, Sen. Iris Rezende, told national CBN radio on Tuesday.
In the Chamber of Deputies, the PMDB's candidate Michel Temer, a whip from the pro-Cardoso wing of the party, has the support of the government.
But Temer faces a growing challenge from two outsiders capitalizing on his difficulties in persuading the PMDB's 102 deputies to take part in a first re-election vote this month.
Analysts said the PMDB, by insisting on fielding candidates in both houses, was seeking to increase its power in Congress to counterbalance the PFL's close relationship with Cardoso.

The PFL, unlike the PMDB, backed the president in his 1994 election campaign and vice-president Marco Maciel is from the PFL. Winning the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate would give the PMBD the third and fourth highest rungs in Brazil's political pecking order.

"The PMDB is upset at being excluded from the inner circle," said Brasilia University politics professor Paulo Kramer. "They are taking advantage of the overlapping of re-election and the congressional elections to strengthen their grip on power."
Kramer said the chances of the PMDB agreeing to take part in a first vote on re-election in the lower house depended on what price the government might offer for their support.
Rezende, the PMDB's candidate in the Senate, has told reporters he twice rejected invitations to become Cardoso's new transport minister in return for withdrawing his candidacy.
He played down concerns that virtually all congressional activity, including progress on key structural reforms, has been halted due to the confusion over re-election.
"The nation is not going to be changed because of a fortnight here or there. People are going to have to be patient," Rezende was quoted as saying in Tuesday's O Globo.
